notes.front: What is GitHub Enterprise Cloud (GHEC)?
notes.back: The GitHub-hosted deployment option of GitHub Enterprise; its key difference from other plans is an enterprise account for managing multiple organizations.
notes.explanation: The enterprise account gives administrators one central point for several organizations, which plans such as GitHub Team do not offer.
notes.example: Like a single GitHub Team organization, but with an enterprise account sitting above many organizations so they can be run together.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Cloud”, “What are the differences between GitHub Enterprise Cloud and other plans?”
notes.evidence: A key difference between GitHub Enterprise Cloud and other GitHub plans is access to an enterprise account, which gives administrators a central point for managing multiple organizations.

notes.front: What is GHE.com?
notes.back: The domain that hosts enterprises using GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, each on its own dedicated subdomain.
notes.explanation: Adopting data residency lets the company choose where its code and data are stored, and its enterprise then lives on a GHE.com subdomain rather than on GitHub.com.
notes.example: Like a company-only address, chosen during onboarding, that developers visit instead of the shared GitHub.com.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency”
notes.evidence: When you adopt GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, you can choose where your company's code and data are stored. Your enterprise will be hosted on a dedicated subdomain of GHE.com.

notes.front: What is GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES)?
notes.back: A self-hosted version of the GitHub platform.
notes.explanation: A business gains more control and avoids issues associated with the public cloud, while developers keep familiar GitHub.com features and workflows.
notes.example: Like GitHub.com, but running as an instance on your own infrastructure and looked after by your own administrators.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”
notes.evidence: GitHub Enterprise Server is a self-hosted version of the GitHub platform. Your business can benefit from increased control and avoid issues associated the public cloud, while your developers can benefit from familiar features and workflows from GitHub.com.

notes.front: In GitHub Enterprise Server, what is a hotpatch?
notes.back: One of the two forms in which GitHub delivers updates for an instance; the other is an upgrade package.
notes.explanation: The administrator is responsible for keeping the instance up to date, and GitHub’s regular updates, including operating-system security patches, arrive in one of these two forms.
notes.example: Like a security fix applied to the running system; if it is eligible, automatic updates can even install it for you. A full upgrade package is the other route.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”, “Keeping GitHub Enterprise Server updated”
notes.evidence: As an administrator, you are responsible for keeping your GitHub Enterprise Server instance up to date. GitHub regularly releases updates for GitHub Enterprise Server, including OS-level security patches. Updates are delivered either as upgrade packages or as hotpatches.

notes.front: What is GitHub Enterprise Server Backup Utilities used for?
notes.back: Taking regular snapshots of a GitHub Enterprise Server instance to back up its configuration and user data.
notes.explanation: It is one of the options GitHub Enterprise Server provides for safeguarding against data loss or service disruptions.
notes.example: Like a scheduled snapshot of a database server, but covering the whole instance’s settings and user data.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”, “Backups and availability”
notes.evidence: GitHub Enterprise Server provides options for safeguarding against data loss or service disruptions. To back up configuration and user data, you can take regular snapshots of your instance using our Backup Utilities system.

notes.front: What is GitHub Connect?
notes.back: A feature you can enable on GitHub Enterprise Server to benefit from features that rely on GitHub.com.
notes.explanation: It is how a self-hosted instance gets features that depend on GitHub.com, such as Dependabot alerts and actions hosted there.
notes.example: Like linking an in-house system to a vendor’s cloud service so it can use something that lives only in that cloud.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub for enterprises”, “About deployment options”
notes.evidence: You can enable GitHub Connect to benefit from features that rely on GitHub.com, such as Dependabot alerts and actions hosted on GitHub.com.

notes.front: In GitHub Enterprise Cloud, what is an enterprise with personal accounts?
notes.back: An enterprise type in which members reach enterprise resources with their own personal accounts, rather than accounts the company provisions.
notes.explanation: The other enterprise type uses Enterprise Managed Users, where the company provisions accounts for users from an external system.
notes.example: Like inviting a developer’s existing GitHub.com account into your organizations, instead of issuing them a new one.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub for enterprises”, “About deployment options”
notes.evidence: To access your resources, members of your enterprise can use their personal account or, if you use Enterprise Managed Users, you will provision accounts for users using an external system.

notes.front: In GitHub Enterprise Cloud, what is an enterprise with managed users?
notes.back: An enterprise type using Enterprise Managed Users: the company provisions and manages members’ accounts on GitHub through its identity provider.
notes.explanation: Each member signs into an account the enterprise creates and manages, and contributions outside the enterprise are restricted.
notes.example: Like a work login issued by a company’s technology team, rather than an account the employee set up for themselves.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Identity and access management fundamentals”, “Authentication with Enterprise Managed Users and federation”
notes.evidence: With Enterprise Managed Users, you provision and manage accounts for your enterprise members on GitHub using your IdP. Each member signs into an account that you create, and your enterprise manages the account. Contributions outside the enterprise are restricted.

notes.front: In GitHub Enterprise Cloud, what is data residency?
notes.back: An option that lets a company choose where its code and data are stored.
notes.explanation: It helps meet specific data residency compliance requirements and makes it easy to keep enterprise work separate from open source work.
notes.example: Like choosing the storage region for a company’s cloud files, but for its whole GitHub enterprise.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency”
notes.evidence: When you adopt GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, you can choose where your company's code and data are stored. Your enterprise will be hosted on a dedicated subdomain of GHE.com. Data residency makes it easy to separate open source and enterprise work, and helps you meet specific data residency compliance requirements.

notes.front: According to GitHub Docs, what does an enterprise account bring together?
notes.back: Administrative tools for access management, policies, billing and more: it is the central point of administration for the business.
notes.explanation: With the tools in one place, enterprise administrators can set up features and policies at scale before deploying them across the business.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”
notes.evidence: An enterprise account is the central point of administration for your business on GitHub. It brings together administrative tools for access management, policies, billing, and more. Enterprise administrators can set up features and policies efficiently at scale before deploying them across the business.

notes.front: A company has twelve organizations under one enterprise. Its administrator wants to set up a policy once and then roll it out across the whole business. Where should the policy be set up?
notes.back: A) In the enterprise account
notes.explanation: The enterprise account is where administrators set up features and policies at scale before deploying them across the business.
notes.choices:
A) In the enterprise account
B) In a settings file committed to one repository
C) In each organization’s settings, one by one
D) In each member’s personal account settings
notes.choicesExplained: C) Organization-by-organization set-up is what the enterprise account saves you from. B) One repository cannot govern the other organizations. D) Personal settings belong to individuals, not to the business.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”
notes.evidence: Enterprise administrators can set up features and policies efficiently at scale before deploying them across the business.

notes.front: Which users does an enterprise contain?
notes.back: All the users who need to access any part of the company’s resources on GitHub.
notes.explanation: Those users can then be grouped into teams and given access to organizations.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”, “Users”
notes.evidence: Your enterprise contains all the users who need to access any part of your company's resources on GitHub. Users can be grouped into teams and given access to organizations.

notes.front: Depending on the enterprise type, what are the two ways users come into an enterprise?
notes.back: They are invited with their existing GitHub account, or dedicated accounts are provisioned for them from a central identity provider.
notes.explanation: The first fits an enterprise with personal accounts; the second fits an enterprise with managed users.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”, “Users”
notes.evidence: Depending on your enterprise type, you will invite users into your enterprise with their existing GitHub account, or provision dedicated accounts from a central identity provider.

notes.front: By default, what kind of role do most users have in an enterprise?
notes.back: A non-administrative role, so they have little reason to interact with the enterprise account itself.
notes.explanation: Administrators can change this for chosen users by granting enterprise roles that give access to specific settings.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”, “Users”
notes.evidence: By default, most users have a non-administrative role in your enterprise, which means they have little reason to interact with the enterprise account itself. However, you can change this by granting enterprise roles that provide access to specific settings.

notes.front: Within an enterprise, what does each organization contain?
notes.back: Its own administrative features, such as audit logs, policies and teams, and the places where non-admins work, such as repositories.
notes.explanation: Repositories, discussions and projects live in organizations, so an organization’s users are the people who need those places to do their jobs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”, “Organizations”
notes.evidence: An enterprise account may contain one or more organizations. Like an enterprise account, an organization account contains its own administrative features such as audit logs, policies, and teams. An organization also contains the places where non-admins typically do their work, such as repositories, discussions, and projects.

notes.front: Organizations can generally be governed consistently from the enterprise account. What can the enterprise delegate to organization administrators instead?
notes.back: Some decisions, such as policy settings.
notes.explanation: Delegation allows more tailored and granular administration than governing everything from the top.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”, “Organizations”
notes.evidence: Generally, you can govern organizations consistently from your enterprise account. To allow for more tailored and granular administration, you can also delegate some decisions, such as policy settings, to organization administrators.

notes.front: Once a team is defined at the enterprise level, what can it be given?
notes.back: Administrative roles, or membership of organizations, where it can receive organization-level roles and repository access.
notes.explanation: One team defined at the top can therefore be added to several organizations and pick up roles and repository access in each.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”, “Teams”
notes.evidence: You can define teams at the enterprise level, then grant them administrative roles or add them to organizations, where they can receive organization-level roles and repository access.

notes.front: In an enterprise, who owns repositories: the enterprise account or its organizations?
notes.back: Organizations. Repositories are not directly accessible under the enterprise account.
notes.explanation: The enterprise can still govern them, by applying one governance model to all repositories that share characteristics.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”, “Repositories”
notes.evidence: Repositories are owned by organizations and are not directly accessible under the enterprise account. However, your enterprise can define custom properties to apply the same governance model to all repositories with shared characteristics.

notes.front: A new administrator plans to create the company’s shared tooling repository directly under the enterprise account, so that no single organization owns it. What should you tell them?
notes.back: C) It cannot be done: repositories are owned by organizations, not by the enterprise account
notes.explanation: Repositories are not directly accessible under the enterprise account, though the enterprise can still govern them across organizations.
notes.choices:
A) It works once the enterprise has more than one organization
B) It works, but only for internal repositories
C) It cannot be done: repositories are owned by organizations, not by the enterprise account
D) It works only in an enterprise with personal accounts
notes.choicesExplained: B) Visibility does not change who owns a repository. A) The number of organizations does not change ownership. D) The enterprise type does not change ownership either.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”, “Repositories”
notes.evidence: Repositories are owned by organizations and are not directly accessible under the enterprise account.

notes.front: What do cost centres let an enterprise do?
notes.back: Allocate spending on GitHub features to specific business units.
notes.explanation: Because the billing structure is defined independently, organizations can be used to group related work or governance requirements instead.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”, “Cost centers”
notes.evidence: Cost centers allow you to allocate spending on GitHub features to specific business units. They let you define your billing structure independently from other parts of the enterprise, so you can focus on using organization accounts to group related work or governance requirements.

notes.front: If an enterprise is billed through Azure, what can its cost centres also do?
notes.back: Bill usage to multiple different Azure subscriptions.
notes.explanation: The feature extends cost centres’ job of allocating spending, for accounts whose billing runs through Azure.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”, “Cost centers”
notes.evidence: If your account is billed through Azure, cost centers also allow you to bill usage to multiple different Azure subscriptions.

notes.front: What are two kinds of policy that enterprise administrators can set to govern how people work?
notes.back: Any two, among others: Copilot policies on features and models; repository policies on deleting, renaming or transferring repositories.
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs lists these as examples of enterprise-wide governance, alongside restrictions on where people can access the enterprise.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”, “Policies”
notes.evidence: Enterprise administrators can set policies to govern how people work across your enterprise, such as: IP allow lists to enforce restrictions on where people can access your enterprise Copilot policies to govern which features and models people can use Repository policies to control who can do things like delete, rename, or transfer repositories

notes.front: In an enterprise account, what can you define to automate a process consistently across organizations?
notes.back: App registrations. You can also install apps that act on the enterprise account itself, such as creating organizations.
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs describes an app as a dedicated identity that gives scoped tokens to external scripts and workflows.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”, “Apps”
notes.evidence: In your enterprise account, you can define app registrations to automate a process consistently across organizations. You can also install apps for automations that take actions on the enterprise account itself, such as creating organizations.

notes.front: A company wants GitHub spending charged separately to its research and marketing departments, without reorganising its organizations around those departments. Which part of the enterprise account fits?
notes.back: D) Cost centres
notes.explanation: Cost centres define the billing structure independently from other parts of the enterprise, so organizations can stay grouped by work.
notes.choices:
A) Teams
B) Organizations
C) Policies
D) Cost centres
notes.choicesExplained: A) Teams manage access to organizations, roles and licences, not spending. B) Reorganising organizations is what the company wants to avoid. C) Policies govern how people work, not who pays.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”, “Cost centers”
notes.evidence: They let you define your billing structure independently from other parts of the enterprise, so you can focus on using organization accounts to group related work or governance requirements.

notes.front: In the GitHub Enterprise plan, what does the enterprise account provide a single place for?
notes.back: Managing teams, granting access, enforcing policies and auditing activity.
notes.explanation: It is the first benefit GitHub Docs lists for the plan, on top of what GitHub Free and GitHub Team give organizations.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub for enterprises”, “Benefits of the GitHub Enterprise plan”
notes.evidence: In addition to the features included with a GitHub Free or GitHub Team plan for organizations, the plan includes: An enterprise account, which provides a single place to manage teams, grant access, enforce policies, and audit activity.

notes.front: Besides SAML authentication, which repository feature does GitHub Docs list among the GitHub Enterprise plan’s additional features?
notes.back: Internal repositories.
notes.explanation: The plan lists them among additional features; the full list is on the GitHub Pricing page.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub for enterprises”, “Benefits of the GitHub Enterprise plan”
notes.evidence: Additional features such as SAML authentication and internal repositories. For a detailed list, see GitHub Pricing.

notes.front: The GitHub Enterprise plan includes extra {{c1::allowances}} for usage-based products such as GitHub Actions.
notes.explanation: GitHub Actions is the example GitHub Docs gives of a usage-based product that gets the extra allowance.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub for enterprises”, “Benefits of the GitHub Enterprise plan”
notes.evidence: Extra allowances for usage-based products such as GitHub Actions.

notes.front: Which two products does the GitHub Enterprise plan give the option to add?
notes.back: GitHub Premium Support and GitHub Copilot Enterprise.
notes.explanation: They are optional additions listed among the plan’s benefits, not part of every GitHub Enterprise purchase.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub for enterprises”, “Benefits of the GitHub Enterprise plan”
notes.evidence: GitHub Premium Support, and GitHub Copilot Enterprise.

notes.front: When a business purchases GitHub Enterprise, which deployment options does it get access to?
notes.back: Both GitHub Enterprise Cloud and GitHub Enterprise Server; it can use one or both.
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs calls both of them deployment options of the one plan, and lets you choose one or both.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub for enterprises”, “About deployment options”
notes.evidence: When you purchase GitHub Enterprise, you get access to both GitHub Enterprise Cloud and GitHub Enterprise Server. You can choose to use one or both of these deployment options.

notes.front: A bank has bought GitHub Enterprise. One division must run GitHub on its own infrastructure; another wants GitHub to host everything. What does GitHub Docs say about this?
notes.back: D) It is possible: the purchase gives access to both GHEC and GHES, and they can use one or both
notes.explanation: Buying GitHub Enterprise gives access to both deployment options, so the self-hosted division can run GHES while the other uses GHEC.
notes.choices:
A) It is not possible: the purchase covers only GHEC
B) Each division must buy a separate plan
C) An enterprise can use only one deployment option at a time
D) It is possible: the purchase gives access to both GHEC and GHES, and they can use one or both
notes.choicesExplained: A) The purchase covers GHES as well as GHEC. B) No second plan is needed for the other option. C) GitHub Docs says you can use one or both.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub for enterprises”, “About deployment options”
notes.evidence: When you purchase GitHub Enterprise, you get access to both GitHub Enterprise Cloud and GitHub Enterprise Server. You can choose to use one or both of these deployment options.

notes.front: With GitHub Enterprise Cloud, who hosts the repositories, and how do new features and bug fixes arrive?
notes.back: GitHub hosts them, and you automatically have access to the latest features and bug fixes.
notes.explanation: This is the opposite of GHES, where you run the instance yourself.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub for enterprises”, “About deployment options”
notes.evidence: Your repositories and other resources are hosted by GitHub, and you'll automatically have access to the latest features and bugfixes.

notes.front: What are two features that GitHub Enterprise Cloud adds to GitHub, from its feature list?
notes.back: Any two, among others: privately published GitHub Pages sites; managed user accounts; repository rulesets; compliance reports.
notes.explanation: These are highlights only; GitHub Docs points to the Pricing page for the full list.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Cloud”
notes.evidence: Privately published GitHub Pages sites Managed user accounts Repository rulesets GitHub's compliance reports For a full list of features included with GitHub Enterprise Cloud, see our Pricing page.

notes.front: How long is the free trial of GitHub Enterprise Cloud?
notes.back: 30 days.
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs offers it as a free way to try GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Cloud”, “Can I try GitHub Enterprise Cloud?”
notes.evidence: You can sign up for a free, 30-day trial of GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

notes.front: With GitHub Enterprise Server, where does the GitHub instance run, and who creates user accounts?
notes.back: You run it, on-premises or on a public cloud service, and you create the user accounts.
notes.explanation: You also authenticate those users, with either built-in authentication or an external system.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub for enterprises”, “About deployment options”
notes.evidence: You run your own GitHub instance, either on-premises or on a public cloud service. You create accounts for users, and authenticate users using either built-in authentication or an external system.

notes.front: What governs a GitHub Enterprise Server instance, and what kind of enterprise does GitHub Docs call it suitable for?
notes.back: Access and security controls you define, such as firewalls and network policies; it suits enterprises subject to regulatory compliance.
notes.explanation: It runs on your own infrastructure, so the controls around it are yours to choose.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”
notes.evidence: GitHub Enterprise Server is suitable for enterprises that are subject to regulatory compliance. It runs on your infrastructure and is governed by access and security controls that you define, such as firewalls, network policies, IAM, monitoring, and VPNs.

notes.front: In what form does GitHub distribute GitHub Enterprise Server, and may you add third-party software to it?
notes.back: As a self-contained virtual appliance on a virtual machine you provision; installing third-party software or changing its operating system is not supported.
notes.explanation: The appliance runs a Linux operating system with a custom application stack that GitHub supplies as a whole.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”, “How do I deploy GitHub Enterprise Server?”
notes.evidence: GitHub distributes GitHub Enterprise Server as a self-contained virtual appliance. After you provision a virtual machine and install the appliance, the instance runs a Linux operating system with a custom application stack. Installing third-party software or making changes to the underlying operating system is not supported.

notes.front: Which on-premises hypervisors are supported for GitHub Enterprise Server?
notes.back: Microsoft Hyper-V, OpenStack KVM and VMware ESXi.
notes.explanation: Only the listed hypervisors are supported for running the appliance on-premises.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”, “Supported on-premises hypervisors”
notes.evidence: Supported on-premises hypervisors Microsoft Hyper-V OpenStack KVM VMware ESXi

notes.front: Which public cloud services are supported for GitHub Enterprise Server?
notes.back: Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud Platform and Microsoft Azure.
notes.explanation: GitHub Enterprise Server can run in a public cloud service as well as on-premises, but only on the supported services.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”, “Supported cloud services”
notes.evidence: Supported cloud services Amazon Web Services (AWS) Google Cloud Platform (GCP) Microsoft Azure

notes.front: On GitHub Enterprise Server, what do automatic updates apply, and do they replace planned full upgrades?
notes.back: Eligible hotpatches, automatically. They do not replace planned full upgrades.
notes.explanation: Administrators can still install upgrade packages or hotpatches manually; automatic updates only cover eligible hotpatches.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”, “Keeping GitHub Enterprise Server updated”
notes.evidence: You can manually install upgrade packages or hotpatches. You can also enable automatic updates to apply eligible hotpatches automatically. Automatic updates do not replace planned full upgrades.

notes.front: A GHES administrator has turned on automatic updates and tells the team that upgrade planning is no longer needed. Is that right?
notes.back: B) No: automatic updates apply only eligible hotpatches and do not replace planned full upgrades
notes.explanation: The administrator remains responsible for keeping the instance current, and full upgrades still have to be planned.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: automatic updates install every upgrade package
B) No: automatic updates apply only eligible hotpatches and do not replace planned full upgrades
C) Yes: GitHub upgrades the appliance remotely once they are on
D) No: automatic updates cannot be turned on for GHES
notes.choicesExplained: A) Upgrade packages are not applied automatically. C) The administrator stays responsible for keeping the instance up to date. D) GHES does offer automatic updates for eligible hotpatches.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”, “Keeping GitHub Enterprise Server updated”
notes.evidence: You can also enable automatic updates to apply eligible hotpatches automatically. Automatic updates do not replace planned full upgrades.

notes.front: Which methods can GitHub Enterprise Server administrators use to set up external authentication?
notes.back: CAS, LDAP or SAML.
notes.explanation: It is one of the administrative options, alongside configuring and monitoring the instance and setting usage policies.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”, “Administrative options”
notes.evidence: Set up external authentication using CAS, LDAP, or SAML Set usage policies to ensure compliance with business rules or regulatory restrictions

notes.front: A manufacturer’s only directory service speaks LDAP, and it wants GitHub sign-in to use that directory directly. Which deployment option lists LDAP as an external authentication method?
notes.back: A) GHES
notes.explanation: GHES administrators can set up external authentication with CAS, LDAP or SAML.
notes.choices:
A) GHES
B) GHEC with an enterprise with personal accounts
C) GHEC with an enterprise with managed users
D) GHEC with data residency
notes.choicesExplained: B) An enterprise with personal accounts adds a SAML access restriction on top of GitHub.com sign-in. C) and D) Managed users authenticate through the company’s identity provider using SAML or OpenID Connect, not LDAP.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”, “Administrative options”
notes.evidence: Set up external authentication using CAS, LDAP, or SAML

notes.front: On GitHub Enterprise Server, what does a passive replica instance improve, and how?
notes.back: Reliability: the instance can fail over to it in the event of a system or network failure.
notes.explanation: It is one of the options for safeguarding against service disruptions, next to backups and active replicas.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”, “Backups and availability”
notes.evidence: To increase reliability, you can configure a passive replica instance to fail over to in the event of a system or network failure.

notes.front: On GitHub Enterprise Server, what do active replicas improve, and how?
notes.back: Performance: they scale the instance for dispersed users or high demand.
notes.explanation: Unlike a passive replica, which waits to take over after a failure, active replicas serve users.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”, “Backups and availability”
notes.evidence: To improve performance, you can configure active replicas to scale the instance for dispersed users or high demand.

notes.front: A GHES instance serves engineers on three continents, and those far from the datacentre find it slow. Which option addresses this?
notes.back: C) Active replicas
notes.explanation: Active replicas scale the instance for dispersed users or high demand, which is the problem here.
notes.choices:
A) A passive replica
B) GitHub Enterprise Server Backup Utilities snapshots
C) Active replicas
D) A hotpatch
notes.choicesExplained: A) A passive replica improves reliability through failover, not performance. B) Backup Utilities snapshots protect configuration and user data. D) A hotpatch is an update, not a way to scale.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”, “Backups and availability”
notes.evidence: To improve performance, you can configure active replicas to scale the instance for dispersed users or high demand.

notes.front: How long is the free trial of GitHub Enterprise Server?
notes.back: 45 days.
notes.explanation: It is longer than the 30-day trial of GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”, “Getting started”
notes.evidence: You can sign up for a free, 45-day trial of GitHub Enterprise Server.

notes.front: Where are most GitHub features released first, before they reach GitHub Enterprise Server?
notes.back: On GitHub.com; they then come to GitHub Enterprise Server through the release process.
notes.explanation: GHES gains new functionality and bug fixes through feature and patch releases.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Server”, “Features and releases”
notes.evidence: GitHub Enterprise Server is constantly improving, with new functionality and bug fixes introduced through feature and patch releases. Most features are released on GitHub.com first, then come to GitHub Enterprise Server through the release process.

notes.front: Developers on a GHES instance want their workflows to use actions that are hosted on GitHub.com. What should the administrator enable?
notes.back: A) GitHub Connect
notes.explanation: GitHub Connect lets a GHES instance benefit from features that rely on GitHub.com, and actions hosted there are one of them.
notes.choices:
A) GitHub Connect
B) A passive replica
C) Data residency
D) GitHub Enterprise Server Backup Utilities
notes.choicesExplained: B) A passive replica is for failover. C) Data residency is a GHEC option, not a GHES feature. D) Backup Utilities takes snapshots; it links nothing to GitHub.com.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub for enterprises”, “About deployment options”
notes.evidence: You can enable GitHub Connect to benefit from features that rely on GitHub.com, such as Dependabot alerts and actions hosted on GitHub.com.

notes.front: When do you choose the enterprise type for GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and what are the two types?
notes.back: While setting up the trial; the types are an enterprise with personal accounts and an enterprise with managed users.
notes.explanation: Setting up the trial is the step where the enterprise type is picked.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Enterprise Cloud”, “About enterprise types”
notes.evidence: While setting up your trial of GitHub Enterprise Cloud, you'll choose an enterprise type. Enterprise with personal accounts Enterprise with managed users

notes.front: In an enterprise with personal accounts, who manages each member’s account, and where else can the member contribute?
notes.back: The member manages it, and can contribute to other enterprises, organizations and repositories on GitHub.com.
notes.explanation: Each person creates and manages their own personal account on GitHub.com, and the enterprise only grants that account access.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Identity and access management fundamentals”, “Authentication through GitHub.com”
notes.evidence: After you grant access to your enterprise, the member can access your enterprise's resources after signing into the account on GitHub.com. The member manages the account, and can contribute to other enterprises, organizations, and repositories on GitHub.com.

notes.front: How do an enterprise with personal accounts and an enterprise with managed users differ in who controls the accounts?
notes.back: Personal accounts: people use their own GitHub.com accounts. Managed users: the enterprise provisions and controls accounts through its IdP.
notes.explanation: With personal accounts an extra identity provider check can optionally be added; with managed users the identity provider controls the accounts themselves.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Identity and access management fundamentals”, “What is IAM for GitHub?”
notes.evidence: To control access to your enterprise's resources, you can allow people to use a personal account on GitHub.com and optionally configure additional SAML access restrictions, or you can provision and control the accounts for your enterprise using your identity provider (IdP) with Enterprise Managed Users.

notes.front: A consultancy wants its developers to keep contributing to open-source projects on GitHub.com with the same account they use for client work in its enterprise. Which enterprise type fits?
notes.back: D) An enterprise with personal accounts
notes.explanation: With personal accounts the member manages the account and can contribute to other enterprises, organizations and repositories on GitHub.com.
notes.choices:
A) An enterprise with managed users
B) GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency
C) Either type, since both let accounts contribute outside the enterprise
D) An enterprise with personal accounts
notes.choicesExplained: A) Managed user accounts have contributions outside the enterprise restricted. B) Data residency uses managed users, with the same restriction. C) Only personal accounts can contribute elsewhere on GitHub.com.
